stem: Why did Ebright begin raising a flock of monarchs in his basement?

A viral disease had wiped out all the monarchs near Reading

stem: Only two butterflies Ebright tagged were recaptured, neither more than seventy-five miles from his home. What does this outcome best show about his tagging work?
options: Monarchs from Reading never migrate to Central America
It gave him too little data to keep him motivated
His tags were too heavy for the butterflies to fly far

stem: The theory was that viceroys copy monarchs because birds find monarchs bad-tasting, yet Ebright's starling ate all the monarchs it could get. Which conclusion is most reasonable from the chapter?

stem: In his senior year, Ebright grew cells from a monarch's wing in a culture. What did this experiment show?
options: Wing cells develop normally without any outside hormone
The gold spots are only ornamental and serve no real purpose

stem: Which sequence correctly traces how Ebright's research led to his theory of cell life?
options: Hormone's structure identified, then spots shown to make a hormone, then cell theory, then wing cells shown to need it
Wing cells shown to need the hormone, then cell theory, then spots shown to make a hormone, then structure identified
Spots shown to make a hormone, then wing cells shown to need it, then structure identified, then cell theory
Spots shown to make a hormone, then structure identified, then wing cells shown to need it, then cell theory
explanation: Correct option: (C). In high school he first showed the gold spots produce a hormone, in his senior year that wing cells need it to form normal scales, after his freshman year at Harvard he identified its chemical structure, and in his junior year X-ray photos of a hormone's structure gave him the theory of cell life. The other orders misplace these steps.
